spark.summary: Apache Spark processes petabyte-scale batch and streaming data across distributed clusters using lazy DAG execution, the Catalyst query optimizer, Tungsten off-heap memory, and Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) over columnar formats like Parquet, Delta Lake, and Apache Iceberg.
spark.keyTakeaway: Almost every slow Spark job comes down to shuffle volume, data skew, or small files—fix those three via broadcast joins, AQE skew handling, and 128 MB–512 MB Parquet/Iceberg compaction before throwing more executors at the cluster.

concept.whyItMatters: Unoptimized Spark pipelines routinely burn 5x–10x more cloud compute than necessary due to wide shuffles, 99% straggler tasks from skewed join keys, or metadata timeouts scanning millions of 50 KB JSON files. Mastering Catalyst, AQE, and columnar table formats turns 2-hour failing nightly ETLs into 10-minute predictable jobs.
whenToUse: Transforming, joining, or aggregating 100 GB to 100+ TB datasets across object storage (S3, GCS, ADLS) using SQL, PySpark, or Scala.
Building medallion (Bronze/Silver/Gold) lakehouse pipelines on Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg with ACID upserts and time travel.
Running near-real-time micro-batch streaming (10s–5m latency) from Kafka into lakehouse tables via Structured Streaming.
whenNotToUse: Small datasets under ~10–20 GB that fit on a single machine where DuckDB, Polars, or PostgreSQL runs 10x faster with zero JVM startup overhead.
Sub-second OLTP point lookups or high-concurrency user-facing dashboards (use PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, ClickHouse, or Pinot instead).
Sub-100ms true event-at-a-time stream processing with complex per-key timers (prefer Apache Flink).
keyPoints: Spark builds a lazy Logical Plan -> Catalyst optimizes (predicate pushdown, projection pruning) -> Physical Plan split at wide shuffles into Stages and Tasks.
Narrow transformations (`filter`, `map`, `withColumn`) stay within one partition; Wide transformations (`groupBy`, `join`, `repartition`) trigger expensive network+disk Shuffles.
Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) in Spark 3+ dynamically coalesces small shuffle partitions, switches Sort-Merge Joins to Broadcast Hash Joins at runtime, and splits skewed partitions.
Always use columnar formats (Parquet/ORC) inside Delta Lake or Iceberg so Spark skips irrelevant row groups via min/max statistics and reads only needed columns.
Python UDFs serialize rows between the JVM and Python workers via Pickle/Arrow; prefer built-in `pyspark.sql.functions` (compiled via Tungsten whole-stage codegen) or Arrow-backed Pandas UDFs.

examples.title: Eliminating a 4-Hour Skewed Clickstream Join
examples.scenario: A daily Spark job joins 800 GB of clickstream events with 20 GB of user profiles on `user_id`. 199 tasks finish in 3 minutes, while 1 task stalls for 4 hours and OOMs because `user_id = NULL` accounts for 35% of traffic.
examples.outcome: Filtering/salting null keys and enabling AQE skew join (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true`) splits the skewed partition across 32 tasks, cutting total job runtime from 4+ hours to 11 minutes.

examples.title: Compacting 500K Small JSON Files into Delta Parquet
examples.scenario: A Kafka sink writes 500,000 x 200 KB JSON files/day to S3; downstream Spark SQL queries spend 12 minutes just listing S3 keys and parsing JSON before computing anything.
examples.outcome: Adding an hourly `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (tenant_id, event_date)` compaction job produces ~128 MB–256 MB Parquet files, dropping query latency from 14 minutes to 22 seconds.

tradeOffs.factor: Broadcast Hash Join vs. Sort-Merge Join
tradeOffs.pro: Broadcast Join (`<= 10 MB` default, tunable up to ~100–256 MB) eliminates the huge fact-table shuffle completely.
tradeOffs.con: Broadcasting a table that exceeds driver/executor memory causes `OutOfMemoryError` or broadcast timeouts.

tradeOffs.pro: `coalesce(N)` avoids a full shuffle by merging existing partitions locally when shrinking partition count.
tradeOffs.con: `coalesce(N)` cannot increase partitions and can create uneven partition sizes or reduce upstream parallelism; `repartition(N)` guarantees even distribution via a full shuffle.

tradeOffs.pro: 4–5 cores and 16–32 GB RAM per executor balances multi-core broadcast sharing with low JVM GC pause times (staying under the 32 GB CompressedOops limit).
tradeOffs.con: Oversized executors (>8 cores, >64 GB heap) suffer long GC stop-the-world pauses and HDFS/S3 I/O contention; tiny 1-core executors duplicate broadcast tables excessively.

failureModes.name: Driver OutOfMemoryError (`collect()` / Large Broadcast)
failureModes.description: Calling `.collect()`, `.toPandas()`, or broadcasting a multi-GB dimension table pulls all partitions into the single Driver JVM.
failureModes.mitigation: Write results directly to S3/Delta (`df.write`), use `.take(100)` for debugging, and keep `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` well below 10% of driver/executor heap.

failureModes.name: Data Skew Stragglers (99/100 Tasks Done)
failureModes.description: A single hot key (`NULL`, `guest`, or a mega-tenant) routes millions of rows to one shuffle partition, causing disk spill and executor OOM.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable AQE skew join (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true`), filter nulls before joining, or salt hot keys (`concat(key, '_', rand() % N)`).

failureModes.name: Small Files Explosion
failureModes.description: Writing 200+ partitions every 30-second micro-batch creates millions of <1 MB files, saturating S3 `LIST` APIs and Driver metadata memory.
failureModes.mitigation: Use AQE partition coalescing, `.repartition(N)` / `maxRecordsPerFile` on write, and scheduled `OPTIMIZE` compaction in Delta Lake or Iceberg.

failureModes.name: Python UDF Serialization Bottleneck
failureModes.description: Standard `@udf` functions force row-by-row JVM-to-Python serialization, bypassing Catalyst and Tungsten whole-stage codegen.
failureModes.mitigation: Rewrite logic with native `pyspark.sql.functions` / Spark SQL expressions, or use vectorized Arrow `@pandas_udf` when Python libraries are mandatory.

commonMistakes: Calling `.cache()` or `.persist()` on massive DataFrames used only once, wasting executor memory and triggering spill.
Leaving `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` at the static default `200` on 50 TB jobs (causing 250 GB/partition) or 500 MB jobs (creating 200 tiny files) without AQE coalescing.
Joining two large tables without checking for `NULL` or default sentinel keys first.
Using `count()` or `show()` inside production ETL loops, forcing repeated full DAG re-evaluations.
Setting executor heap above `32 GB`, losing JVM Compressed Oops and triggering multi-second GC pauses.

sections.content:
## The idea

Apache Spark is a distributed compute engine built around **immutable distributed datasets** (DataFrames/Datasets) and **lazy DAG execution**. Rather than executing transformations line by line, Spark records a Logical Plan and waits for an **Action** (`write`, `count`, `collect`).

When an action triggers, the **Catalyst Optimizer** applies rule-based and cost-based optimizations—pushing `WHERE` filters down into Parquet footers (**Predicate Pushdown**) and dropping unused columns (**Column Pruning**). Next, the **Tungsten** engine compiles physical operators into tight Java bytecode (**Whole-Stage Codegen**) operating on off-heap binary `UnsafeRow` buffers to avoid JVM object/GC overhead.

Execution splits into **Stages** wherever data must cross the network (**Shuffle**). Narrow stages pipeline `filter -> map -> project` in memory at ~200–500 MB/s per core; wide stages write sorted shuffle blocks to local NVMe and fetch them across executors.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a **500 GB Parquet Orders + 8 MB Stores** aggregation in Spark 3.5 with AQE enabled:

1. **Logical & Catalyst Optimization:** `orders.filter(col('dt') == '2026-11-12').join(stores, 'store_id').groupBy('region').agg(sum('amount'))`. Catalyst pushes `dt = '2026-11-12'` to partition pruning (reading only 15 GB of Parquet instead of 500 GB) and prunes 42 unused columns down to 3 (`store_id`, `amount`, `dt`).
2. **Stage 1 (Map-Side Broadcast + Partial Agg):** Because `stores` is `8 MB` (`< 10 MB` `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`), the Driver broadcasts `stores` as a read-only hash map to all executors. Each task scans a `128 MB` Parquet split, probes the local `stores` hash map (**zero shuffle on `orders`**), and performs a **map-side partial `sum(amount)`** per `region`.
3. **Shuffle Write & AQE Coalesce:** Executors write tiny partial sums (`< 50 MB` total across the cluster) into 200 shuffle partitions. AQE inspects shuffle statistics at the stage boundary and **coalesces 200 partitions down to 2** (`64 MB` target size).
4. **Stage 2 (Final Agg & Write):** Just 2 tasks merge the partial sums and write 2 clean, compacted Delta Parquet output files.

sections.content:
## AQE and key configuration levers

Spark 3's **Adaptive Query Execution (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true`)** eliminates most manual partition tuning by re-planning between stages using real runtime byte counts:

- **Dynamic Partition Coalescing (`coalescePartitions.enabled=true`):** Combines small post-shuffle partitions toward `advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes` (`64 MB` default), preventing thousands of near-empty tasks.
- **Skew Join Optimization (`skewJoin.enabled=true`):** Automatically detects shuffle partitions exceeding `skewedPartitionFactor` (`5x` median) and `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (`256 MB`), splitting them into sub-partitions and duplicating the matching right-side partition.
- **Dynamic Join Strategy Switching:** If a filtered table shrinks below `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (`10 MB`) at runtime, AQE downgrades a Sort-Merge Join to a Broadcast Hash Join on the fly.

## Common bottlenecks and exact fixes

| Symptom in Spark UI | Root Cause | Primary Fix | Key Config / Pattern |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **99/100 tasks finish; 1 task stalls** | Hot key (`NULL` / bot ID) causing partition skew | Enable AQE skew join, filter nulls, or salt keys | `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true` |
| **Huge Shuffle Read/Write (>TB)** | Sort-Merge Join on small dim table or wide `groupBy` | Broadcast small tables; pre-filter before join | `broadcast(dim_df)`, `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` |
| **Driver OOM during query** | `.collect()`, `.toPandas()`, or huge broadcast | Write to storage; limit driver collection | Avoid `collect()`, tune `spark.driver.memory` |
| **Slow S3 listing / 100k tasks** | Millions of tiny <1 MB files | Compact tables; tune partition bytes on write | Delta `OPTIMIZE`, `maxPartitionBytes=134217728` |
| **High GC Time (>10% task time)** | Executor heap >32 GB or Python UDF object churn | Use 4–5 core / 16–24 GB executors; native SQL | `spark.executor.cores=4`, `spark.executor.memory=20g` |

## Failure modes

- **Shuffle FetchFailedException:** When Spot/Preemptible executors are reclaimed mid-job, local shuffle files vanish and Spark must recompute upstream stages. Use External Shuffle Service, Push-Based Shuffle, or on-demand nodes for shuffle-heavy stages.
- **Spill-Induced Disk Full:** A skewed `groupBy` or `join` spills hundreds of GBs to `/tmp` on executor nodes, crashing multiple tasks on the same host.
- **Broadcast Timeout (`300s`):** Broadcasting a table that triggers a slow upstream scan times out (`spark.sql.broadcastTimeout`). Materialize or increase timeout only after verifying size.
- **Cross-Join Explosion:** Omitting or mis-typing a join condition triggers a Cartesian product (`N * M` rows) unless `spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled` is kept `false`.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Lakehouse formats: Delta Lake and Iceberg
sections.content:
## Lakehouse formats: Delta Lake and Iceberg

Raw Parquet directories lack atomicity: a failed Spark job leaves half-written files that corrupt downstream readers. **Delta Lake** and **Apache Iceberg** solve this by adding a transactional metadata layer (`_delta_log` JSON/checkpoint files or Iceberg manifest snapshots):

- **ACID Isolation:** Readers always see a consistent snapshot while writers execute `MERGE INTO` upserts or `DELETE`s.
- **Data Skipping & Z-Ordering:** File-level min/max column statistics let Spark skip 95%+ of Parquet files on selective `WHERE` filters.
- **Schema Evolution & Time Travel:** Safely add columns or roll back a bad pipeline write (`VERSION AS OF 42`) without restoring backups.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Confirm dataset size justifies Spark (>20 GB) rather than single-node DuckDB/Polars.
- [ ] Enable AQE (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true`) and skew join handling in Spark 3+.
- [ ] Replace Python `@udf`s with built-in `pyspark.sql.functions` or Arrow `@pandas_udf`.
- [ ] Size executors to 4–5 cores and <= 24–30 GB heap (staying below the 32 GB CompressedOops boundary).
- [ ] Store tables in Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg (Parquet + Snappy/Zstd) and compact files to 128 MB–512 MB.
- [ ] Inspect the Spark UI SQL/Stages tab for `Shuffle Read`, `Spill (Disk)`, and `Max Task Time` vs. `Median Task Time`.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Apache Spark processes petabyte-scale batch and streaming data across distributed clusters using lazy DAG execution, the Catalyst query optimizer, Tungsten off-heap memory, and Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) over columnar formats like Parquet, Delta Lake, and Apache Iceberg.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Shuffle & AQE Coordinator applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Delta / Iceberg Storage.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Delta / Iceberg Storage experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Write results directly to S3/Delta (`df.write`), use `.take(100)` for debugging, and keep `autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` well below 10% of driver/executor heap.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Almost every slow Spark job comes down to shuffle volume, data skew, or small files—fix those three via broadcast joins, AQE skew handling, and 128 MB–512 MB Parquet/Iceberg compaction before throwing more executors at the cluster.
Avoid trap: Calling `.cache()` or `.persist()` on massive DataFrames used only once, wasting executor memory and triggering spill.
Avoid trap: Leaving `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` at the static default `200` on 50 TB jobs (causing 250 GB/partition) or 500 MB jobs (creating 200 tiny files) without AQE coalescing.
When to reach for it: Transforming, joining, or aggregating 100 GB to 100+ TB datasets across object storage (S3, GCS, ADLS) using SQL, PySpark, or Scala.
When to reach for it: Building medallion (Bronze/Silver/Gold) lakehouse pipelines on Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg with ACID upserts and time travel.

putItTogether.title: Putting Spark Data Engineering Together
putItTogether.summary: Almost every slow Spark job comes down to shuffle volume, data skew, or small files—fix those three via broadcast joins, AQE skew handling, and 128 MB–512 MB Parquet/Iceberg compaction before throwing more executors at the cluster.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Spark Data Engineering before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Filtering/salting null keys and enabling AQE skew join (`spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true`) splits the skewed partition across 32 tasks, cutting total job runtime from 4+ hours to 11 minutes.
